quote: Ist diese Fläche topologisch dadurch völlig bestimmt?
english: Is this surface thereby completely determined topologically?
topic: Hilbert notes the problem of bending a 2n-gon with identified sides into a regular surface, sketches the Boy surface, Klein bottle and ring surface as polygon identifications, proposes realizing Boy's surface algebraically, asks questions about surfaces with prescribed double curves and about embedding projective space in 4-space, and begins a remark on classifying partial differential equations by their characteristic equation.

triage.modern_statement: This is my best reading of the page context, where Hilbert asks about surfaces with prescribed double curves. Take a closed surface (for example the projective plane, as in Boy's surface) immersed generically in R^3 or S^3. Its self-intersection set is the double curve together with its triple points, and it has a given combinatorial pattern. Does that pattern fix the immersed surface up to homeomorphism or ambient isotopy? For the Boy case: is every generic immersion of RP^2 whose self-intersection set is connected and has one triple point equivalent to Boy's surface?
triage.answered_by: Sue Goodman and Marek Kossowski, 'Immersions of the projective plane with one triple point', Differential Geometry and its Applications 27(4), 2009, pp. 527–542. Related background: Pinkall showed every immersion of RP^2 is regularly homotopic to Boy's surface or its mirror image, and Banchoff (1974) showed the number of triple points is congruent to the Euler characteristic mod 2. For the Boy case the answer is no: the double-point structure alone does not determine the surface. There are exactly two models, Boy's surface and the 'Girl's surface', plus their mirror images.

evidence.claim: Goodman–Kossowski abstract: besides Boy's immersion there is another immersion of the projective plane whose self-intersection set is equivalent to Boy's, but whose image is not homeomorphic to Boy's. Any C∞ generic immersion of RP^2 into S^3 with a connected self-intersection set and a single triple point is ambiently isotopic to exactly one of these two models or their mirrors.
The same abstract says Pinkall showed every immersion of the projective plane is homotopic through immersions to Boy's immersion or its mirror.
There is a second, homeomorphically different way to model the projective plane with the same set of intersection lines as Boy's surface; it has been named Girl's surface.
Boy's surface was discovered in 1901 by Werner Boy, on an assignment from Hilbert. It is one of the two possible immersions of the real projective plane with only a single triple point.

A further 2014 paper by Goodman and Howard, published in Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, extends the study to generic maps of the projective plane with a single triple point.

triage.why: The note says 'this surface' without naming which one, so my reading is an assumption based on the page topic (surfaces with prescribed double curves, Boy's surface). Under that reading the question has a clear modern answer. For RP^2 with a connected double curve and one triple point, Goodman–Kossowski (2009) showed the surface is not determined: two inequivalent models exist, Boy's and Girl's surface, up to mirror image. The question is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Self-intersections of immersed surfaces are still being studied, for example the 2014 Goodman–Howard paper and a 2025 arXiv paper (2506.21130) on immersed spheres with no triple points. If Hilbert meant a different surface or data, such as the polygon identifications, this match would not apply.
